title: b, d, f, k, l, m, n, p, s, t, z sound as in English
body: These letters are close to English, with small differences: p, t and k have no puff of air after them, t and d are made with the tongue touching the teeth, and s is always “s” as in “sun”, never “z”.

title: Stress falls on the second-to-last syllable
body: Almost every Polish word is stressed on the next-to-last syllable, so you can read stress straight off the page. The stress moves when an ending adds a syllable: telefon “te-LE-fon”, but telefonu “te-le-FO-noo”. One-syllable words such as nie or się usually lean on the word next to them.

title: a sounds like “a” in “father”, but short
body: Polish a is always an open, short “a”, never the “a” of “cat” or “late”. It keeps this sound in every syllable, stressed or not.

title: e sounds like “e” in “bed”, even at the end of a word
body: e is always the short “e” of “bed”, never “ee”. Polish has no silent e: a final e is clearly said, as in mleko or nie.

title: o sounds like “o” in British “lot”
body: o is a short, open “o”, never the “oh” glide of English “go”. It keeps this sound in unstressed syllables too.

title: w sounds like “v”
body: Polish w is the English “v”. It turns into “f” after voiceless consonants, before them and at the end of a word (see those rules).

title: i sounds like “ee” in “see”
body: When i is a vowel of its own it is a clear “ee”, a little shorter than in English. Before another vowel it usually only softens the consonant in front of it (see the rules for si, ci, ni and for kie, mia, wie).

title: y sounds like “i” in “bit”, never “ee”
body: y is always a vowel in Polish, like the “i” in “bit” said a little further back. Keep it apart from i: my “mih” means “we”, but mi “mee” means “to me”.

title: r is rolled or tapped
body: r is a quick tap or roll of the tip of the tongue, as in Spanish or Scottish English. Always pronounce it, also before consonants and at the end of a word. (rz is a different sound.)

title: u and ó both sound like “oo” in “boot”
body: u and ó are two spellings of the same sound, a short “oo”. ó is never an “o” sound, so który and kura have the same vowel.

title: ł sounds like “w” in “water”
body: ł is the English “w”, made with rounded lips. It is never an “l” in modern standard Polish.

title: j sounds like “y” in “yes”
body: j is always the “y” of “yes”, never the English “j”. After a vowel it forms a glide, like “oy” in “boy”.

title: ń and ni sound like “ny” in “canyon”
body: ń is a soft “n”, like “ny” in “canyon”. Before a vowel it is written ni, and the i is not said separately: nie is one syllable. At the end of a word, as in dzień, it is a short soft “n” with a hint of “y”.

title: i before a vowel after b, p, m, w, k, g, l sounds like “y”
body: After consonants other than s, c, z, n and dz, an i in front of a vowel is a short “y” glide, not a separate syllable: miasto has two syllables, “MYAS-to”. Borrowed words such as radio and historia work the same way.

title: ś and si sound like a soft “sh”
body: ś is a soft “sh”, made with the middle of the tongue raised and the lips spread, softer than sz. Before a vowel it is written si, and the i is not said separately: siedem has two syllables.

title: g is always hard, as in “go”
body: g is always the “g” of “go”, also before e and i. It is never the “j” sound of “gem”.

title: ć and ci sound like a soft “ch”
body: ć is a soft “ch”, as in “cheese” said with the lips spread, softer than cz. Before a vowel it is written ci, and the i is not said separately: ciasto has two syllables.

title: Voiced consonants before p, t, k, s, sz, ch… turn voiceless
body: Before a voiceless consonant, b, d, g, w, z, ż/rz, ź become p, t, k, f, s, sh, soft sh. This also happens across words with the little words w and z: w pracy “f PRA-tsih”, z Polski “s POL-skee”.

title: c sounds like “ts” in “cats”
body: c on its own is always “ts”, also at the start and end of a word. It is never “k” or “s”. (cz, ch and ci are different sounds, see their rules.)

title: rz and ż both sound like “s” in “measure”
body: rz and ż are two spellings of one sound, the “zh” in “measure” or “vision”. So morze (sea) and może (maybe) sound the same.

title: sz sounds like “sh” in “shop”
body: sz is one sound, a firm “sh” said with the tongue pulled slightly back. Compare the softer ś (see its rule).

title: cz sounds like “ch” in “church”
body: cz is one sound, a firm “ch” said with the tongue pulled slightly back. Compare the softer ć (see its rule).

title: Voiced consonants at the end of a word turn voiceless
body: At the end of a word b, d, g, w, z, ż/rz, ź, dz are said as p, t, k, f, s, sh, soft sh, ts. So the very common ending -ów sounds “oof”.

title: dź and dzi sound like a soft “j” in “jeep”
body: dź is a soft “j”, as in “jeep” said with the lips spread, softer than dż. Before a vowel it is written dzi, and the i is not said separately: dziecko has two syllables.

title: ch and h both sound like “ch” in Scottish “loch”
body: ch and h are the same sound: a breathy “kh” from the back of the mouth, softer than in German. It is never the “ch” of “church”.

title: ę at the end of a word sounds like a plain “e”
body: In everyday speech a final ę is said like an ordinary e, with at most a light nasal touch. This covers very common words such as się and the -ę of many verbs and nouns.

title: rz after p, t, k, ch sounds like “sh”
body: Right after p, t, k and ch, rz loses its voice and is said “sh”. This makes very common words like przez, przy and trzy start with “psh” and “tsh”.

title: ą and ę before t, d, c, ć, k, g become “on/en” or “ong/eng”
body: Before t, d, c, cz, ć and dz the nasal vowels become a plain vowel plus a clear “n”; before k and g they become a vowel plus “ng” as in “finger”.

title: ą is a nasal “on”
body: ą is an “o” said through the nose, as in French “bon”; the “n” is not fully pronounced. At the end of a word it sounds like a nasal “own”. Before p, b, t, d, k, g and c it changes (see the next rules).

title: dz sounds like “ds” in “adds”
body: dz is one sound, the voiced partner of c: “dz” as in “adds”. (dzi, dź and dż are different sounds, see their rules.)

title: w after p, t, k, s, sz, cz, ch sounds like “f”
body: Right after a voiceless consonant, w is not voiced and is said “f”. This is why twój sounds “tfooy” and czwartek starts with “chf”.

title: ź and zi sound like a soft “zh”
body: ź is a soft version of the “s” in “measure”, softer than ż. Before a vowel it is written zi, and the i is not said separately: zima has two syllables.

title: Double consonants are held longer
body: A doubled letter is said as a long consonant, not as a single one: Anna has a held “n”, and lekko a held “k”. Each letter of the pair is clearly heard.

title: szcz sounds like “shch” in “fresh cheese”
body: szcz is simply sz followed by cz. Say it like the joined sounds in “fresh cheese”.

title: ę inside a word is a nasal “en”
body: ę is an “e” said through the nose; the “n” is not fully pronounced. Before l and ł it loses the nasal sound and is a plain “e”, as in zaczęła. At the end of a word and before p, b, t, d, k, g and c it changes (see those rules).

title: Final ł after a consonant is usually silent
body: In everyday speech a ł at the end of a word after another consonant is normally dropped, as in past-tense forms like mógł and poszedł. Careful speakers may still say a light “w”.

title: ą and ę before p or b become “om” and “em”
body: Before p and b the nasal vowels turn into a plain vowel plus a clear “m”.

title: -liśmy, -łyście and -łabym endings do not move the stress
body: In past-tense forms with -śmy or -ście, and conditional forms with -bym, -byś or -by, the stress stays where it was before the ending was added. So it lands on the third-to-last syllable: byli “BIH-lee”, but byliśmy “BIH-lee-shmih”.

title: Voiceless consonants before b, d, g, ż, z turn voiced
body: The opposite also happens: before b, d, g, z, ż, ź and dz, the consonants k, t, p, s, ś, cz, ć become g, d, b, z, ź, dż, dź. (w does not cause this.)

title: dż sounds like “j” in “jam”
body: dż is the firm “j” of “jam”, the voiced partner of cz. It is rare and appears mostly in borrowed words and in verbs like jeździć → jeżdżę.

title: Words like muzyka and matematyka stress the third-to-last syllable
body: Many borrowed words ending in -yka or -ika (school subjects, Ameryka, Afryka) are stressed one syllable earlier than usual, in the forms -ka, -ki, -ce, -kę and -ką. Polish names such as Weronika or Monika follow the normal rule.
